title: Serengeti Field Trip for University Groups: Research Sites, Permits and Camp Logistics
meta_title: Serengeti Field Trip: Plan a University Ecology Course
meta_description: Plan a Serengeti field trip for university students: research permits, the best months, a 10-day route from Arusha and per-student park fees.
excerpt: A Serengeti field trip for university groups: when research permits apply, which season suits your course, a 10-day route via Seronera and real park fees per student.
content:
A Serengeti field trip gives university groups a working lesson in savannah ecology: the migration, predator-prey dynamics, grazing succession and long-term research all in one ecosystem. Plan nine to twelve days from Arusha, base yourselves near Seronera and time the trip to the season that fits your course.

The hard part for a lecturer is not the wildlife. It is the paperwork, the distances, keeping 20 or more students on schedule and costing it per head so the department signs off. Our student and study tour safaris are built around exactly that, and this guide covers permits, timing, a sample route, real park fees and how we run a university group safely.

Quick Facts

  • Best length: 9 to 12 days on the ground, starting and ending in Arusha
  • Research base: Seronera in the central Serengeti, about 327 km from Arusha by road or about an hour by air
  • Study themes: migration ecology, predator-prey behaviour, grazing succession, disease and human-wildlife conflict
  • Park fees: up to US$82.60 per adult per 24 hours in the Serengeti (checked November 2026)
  • Research permits: needed from COSTECH only if students collect data for a project or publication
  • Best months: January to February for calving, June to October for dry roads and river crossings

Why Is the Serengeti Worth the Distance for a University Field Trip?

The Serengeti is worth the distance because few ecosystems are studied as long or as thoroughly. Research has been running here since the days of Bernhard Grzimek, so students can compare what they see from the vehicle with decades of published work on the same lions, wildebeest and grasslands.

On a Serengeti field trip a biology group can test whether wildebeest, zebra and gazelle graze the same plains in sequence, and a conservation group can see how a protected area works beside farming and pastoral land.

What can students study on a Serengeti field trip?

Most university groups build a Serengeti field trip around four themes: migration, and why the wildebeest move in a loop driven by rain and grass; predation, with lion, cheetah, hyena and leopard present year round; vegetation, from short-grass plains to acacia woodland; and people, through grazing, fire, disease and the conservation areas around the park.

The Serengeti Wildlife Research Centre at Seronera

The Serengeti Wildlife Research Centre sits at Seronera and is run by the Tanzania Wildlife Research Institute. According to TAWIRI's own page on the centre, it has a wildlife veterinary laboratory, a library holding around 50 years of northern Tanzania research, a zoology museum and a herbarium. It supervises field practicals for Tanzanian universities and gives talks on its research to visitors when asked.

On a Serengeti field trip, a researcher's talk on the long-term lion study or wild dog work can be the best hour of the week. Ask early and stay flexible, because the scientists' own fieldwork comes first.

Do University Students Need a Research Permit in Tanzania?

University students on a Serengeti field trip need a research permit only if they collect data for a project, dissertation or publication. A teaching trip where students observe, take notes and complete set exercises normally travels on ordinary tourist visas, with park fees paid as visitors.

Research is a different matter. Tanzania's Commission for Science and Technology (COSTECH) issues research permits, and its guidelines ask for applications at least three months before the work starts. The application fee is US$50 and the permit fee US$300 per person, and the Tanzania High Commission research permit page also lists a US$120 residence permit fee (all checked November 2026). Wildlife research also needs ethical clearance from TAWIRI.

COSTECH's guidelines also say short-term foreign student researchers should be affiliated with a recognised Tanzanian university or research institution. If one student plans to gather thesis data, involve your research office early. We handle the field side of a Serengeti field trip, not research permit applications.

Visas, yellow fever and health

Most nationalities pay US$50 for a single-entry Tanzania visa, while US citizens pay US$100 for a multiple-entry visa (checked October 2026). Our Tanzania visa guide explains how to apply online. Students arriving from or transiting through Kenya need a yellow fever certificate, as set out on our yellow fever requirements page. The Serengeti is a malaria area, so every student should see a travel clinic before departure.

When Should a University Group Visit the Serengeti?

A Serengeti field trip should run when your academic calendar and your study theme overlap. January and February bring calving on the southern plains, June to October gives dry roads and the northern river crossings, and the long rains of April and May suit vegetation work but slow the driving.

The table shows what each season offers a university group. The migration loop moves slightly every year with the rain, so treat the zones as a guide and let us check recent movements before you fix the route. For the full calendar, see our Great Migration month by month guide.

MonthsWhere the herds usually areGood for studying
January to MarchSouthern plains around NdutuCalving, predator behaviour, short-grass ecology
April to MayMoving from the south towards the centreVegetation growth, rainfall response, birdlife (some roads difficult)
June to JulyWestern corridor and central SerengetiMovement corridors, river ecosystems, crocodile and herd interaction
August to OctoberNorthern Serengeti and the Mara RiverRiver crossings, scavenger ecology, dry-season water stress
November to DecemberHeading south again after the short rainsMigration in motion, early-season grass recovery

Calving season is the richest time for predator studies, because cheetah and hyena concentrate around the herds. Our Serengeti calving season guide explains the weeks in more detail if your semester break falls in January or February.

A Sample 10-Day Serengeti Field Trip Itinerary

A ten-day Serengeti field trip from Arusha gives a university group three teaching landscapes before the main fieldwork at Seronera. The route below runs by road on the way in and offers a flight from Seronera to Arusha on the way out, which saves a full day of driving.

DayWhereField focus
Day 1Arrive at Kilimanjaro International Airport, transfer to ArushaSafety briefing, field kit check, course introduction
Day 2Tarangire National ParkElephant density, baobab and acacia woodland, dry-season water use
Day 3Ngorongoro CraterCaldera geology, a closed ecosystem, black rhino conservation
Day 4Olduvai Gorge, then into the Serengeti to SeroneraHuman evolution in context, the short-grass plains at Naabi Hill
Day 5SeroneraResearch centre talk (by request), kopje habitats, predator watch
Day 6SeroneraHerbivore counts on set routes, evening data session
Day 7Seasonal zone (south, west or north)Migration herds and the predators following them
Day 8Seasonal zoneRepeat counts or behaviour sampling, group presentations
Day 9Fly Seronera to Arusha, or drive back to KaratuWrite-up time in camp or lodge
Day 10ArushaDebrief and departure

Shorter versions of this Serengeti field trip exist. Our 6 Days 5 Nights Northern Tanzania Safari covers Tarangire, the Serengeti and the Ngorongoro Crater and can be stretched with extra Seronera days, while the 8 Day Midrange Tanzania Safari adds Lake Eyasi for groups with an anthropology angle. Schools looking at younger pupils should read our Tanzania school trip guide instead.

How Much Does a Serengeti Field Trip Cost Per Student?

A Serengeti field trip usually costs roughly US$250 to US$350 per student per day on a camping basis and US$400 to US$600 per day with mid-range lodges, excluding international flights. These are our estimates. University students are adults, so every student pays full adult park rates.

Park fees are the largest fixed cost and they do not fall with group size. The table shows entry fees per student on the ten-day route above, using non-resident adult rates including VAT. Our Tanzania park fees guide lists every park, and you should confirm current rates before you set a budget.

FeePer student (adult rate)Notes
Tarangire, 1 dayUS$59.00Entry for 24 hours
Ngorongoro Conservation Area, 3 entriesUS$212.40US$70.80 each; the road route crosses the area three times
Crater service feeAbout US$49US$295 per vehicle per descent, shared by six
Olduvai GorgeUS$35.40Museum and gorge viewpoint
Serengeti, 4 x 24 hoursUS$330.40US$82.60 each in high season
Total park feesAbout US$686Before campsite or concession fees (checked November 2026)

Accommodation is where a Serengeti field trip budget has room to move. Camping with a mobile crew keeps costs lowest, while tented camps and lodges cost more but give students power and desks for evening write-ups. Lodges and camps inside the park also charge a nightly concession fee of roughly US$59 to US$71 per person on top of entry.

What pushes the cost of a Serengeti field trip up or down?

Four things move the price most: the season, nights inside the park, students per vehicle and whether you fly out of Seronera. Full vehicles lower the per-head cost, and travelling outside June to October usually brings lower lodge rates. Lecturers and teaching assistants pay the same fees as students, so build their costs into the per-student price.

Vehicles, Camps and Safety for a University Group

A university group on a Serengeti field trip travels best in 4x4 Land Cruisers with pop-up roofs, six or seven students per vehicle so everyone has a window seat. A group of 24 students and two lecturers therefore needs four or five vehicles, each with its own guide and radio contact with the others.

Running a private group trip, rather than joining a scheduled safari with strangers, is what makes fieldwork possible. On a private Serengeti field trip your vehicles stop where the lecturer wants, stay at a sampling point as long as needed and start at dawn for counts. You can read more about how we structure these trips on our group safaris page and our guide to how to organise a group safari.

Rooming and camp life

On a camping trip students share two-person tents, with a cook and camp crew travelling ahead to set up. Lodges usually offer twin and triple rooms. Ask for a mess tent or meeting room for evening lectures and data entry. Our Serengeti camps guide explains which areas suit which season.

Keeping students safe in the field

Camps in the Serengeti are unfenced, so the rules are simple and firm: no walking outside camp without a ranger, an escort after dark and nobody leaving a vehicle during game drives except at marked sites. Every student needs travel insurance that covers medical evacuation, and our Flying Doctors page explains how air evacuation cover works. Agree a staff-to-student ratio with your university before you travel.

Insider Tips

  • Start permits first: if any student will collect thesis data, begin the COSTECH process at least three months out
  • Ask about a talk: request a researcher talk at Seronera when you confirm dates, not on arrival
  • Set fixed routes: repeat the same drive at the same hour on two days so counts can be compared
  • Bring power banks: campsites often have no charging; lodges usually do
  • Pack for cold mornings: dawn at Seronera and on the crater rim is cool; see our Tanzania packing list
  • Fly out if you can: the Seronera to Arusha flight saves a long day on the road for write-ups

Frequently Asked Questions

Do students need a research permit for a Serengeti field trip?

A Serengeti field trip that only observes and teaches runs on ordinary visas and park fees. Any project collecting data for a dissertation or publication needs a COSTECH research permit, applied for at least three months ahead, with US$50 and US$300 fees, plus TAWIRI clearance for wildlife studies. Confirm the rules before you travel.

How long should a Serengeti field trip be?

A Serengeti field trip for a university group works best at nine to twelve days on the ground. That allows two travel days from Arusha, a day each in Tarangire and the Ngorongoro Crater, three or four days around Seronera and two days in the zone where the migration is that month. Anything shorter turns fieldwork into sightseeing from a moving vehicle.

How much does a Serengeti field trip cost per student?

A Serengeti field trip usually costs roughly US$250 to US$350 per student per day on a camping basis and US$400 to US$600 per day with mid-range lodges, excluding international flights. These are estimates. Park fees alone come to about US$690 per student on a ten-day northern circuit route, before any campsite or concession fees (checked November 2026).

Can a university group visit the Serengeti Wildlife Research Centre?

The Serengeti Wildlife Research Centre at Seronera, run by TAWIRI, says it gives scientific talks on past and ongoing research to visitors, tailored to the group. A university group should request a talk well before travelling, through TAWIRI, and treat it as possible rather than guaranteed, because researchers' fieldwork comes first. The centre also has a library, a zoology museum and a herbarium.

What is the best month for a Serengeti field trip?

The best month for a Serengeti field trip depends on what you want to study. January and February suit calving and predator studies on the southern plains, June to October gives dry roads and the northern river crossings, and the April and May rains suit vegetation work but make some tracks hard to use. Most university groups travel in June to September or January to February.

Final Thoughts

A Serengeti field trip rewards the planning it needs: pick the season that matches your course, sort research permits early if anyone is collecting data, and give the group at least four days around Seronera. Done that way, students come home with real field data and a far clearer picture of how a savannah ecosystem works.
